title: Problem Overview
content: **Erdős Problem #787** (the Erdős-Moser problem) asks: given any n-set A ⊆ ℤ, how large a subset B ⊆ A can we guarantee such that no sum b₁ + b₂ of distinct elements of B lies in A? The function g(n) is this worst-case guarantee. Current best bounds: (log n)^{1+c} ≪ g(n) ≪ exp(√(log n)). The exact order is unknown.
mathContext: This is distinct from the classical sum-free problem (where b₁+b₂ ∉ B). Here sums must avoid the ambient set A, a weaker but still structurally rich condition. Choi showed WLOG we can work with A ⊆ ℤ. The enormous gap between lower and upper bounds makes this one of the central open problems in additive combinatorics.

title: Definitions and Basic Results
content: **IsSumAvoidingIn A B** requires B ⊆ A and ∀ distinct b₁, b₂ ∈ B, b₁+b₂ ∉ A. **maxSumAvoidingSize** takes the supremum over all sum-avoiding subsets. **HasSumAvoidingSubset A k** asserts ∃ B with IsSumAvoidingIn A B and |B| ≥ k. **g** (axiom) and **g_spec** capture the extremal function. **empty_is_sum_avoiding** and **singleton_is_sum_avoiding** are proved: the empty set is vacuously sum-avoiding, and singletons have no two distinct elements to form sums.
mathContext: The function g is axiomatized rather than defined because its definition requires an infimum over all n-element integer subsets, which is not directly constructible in Lean. The specification g_spec asserts g(n) is the largest k with the universal property and not k+1 — capturing its extremality.

title: Historical Bounds: Klarner, Choi, Ruzsa
content: **klarner_lower_bound** (axiom): g(n) ≥ c·log n via greedy construction. **choi_1971_upper_bound** (axiom): g(n) ≤ n^{2/5+ε} for any ε > 0 and large n. **ruzsa_2005_upper_bound** (axiom): g(n) ≤ K·exp(√(log n)), the current best upper bound, dramatically improving Choi.
mathContext: Klarner's greedy argument works by noting each element added to B blocks at most O(|B|) future candidates, yielding exponential capacity. Choi's upper bound constructs sets where large subsets inevitably have additive coincidences. Ruzsa's exp(√log n) arises from sophisticated probabilistic constructions and remains unimproved since 2005.

title: Modern Bounds: Sanders and Beker
content: **sanders_2021_lower_bound** (axiom): g(n) ≥ K·(log n)^{1+c} for some c > 0, a breakthrough beyond the logarithmic barrier. **bekerExponent** = 1 + 1/68 ≈ 1.0147. **beker_2025_lower_bound** (axiom): g(n) ≥ K·(log n)^{1+1/68-ε} for any ε > 0 and large n, refining Sanders' result with a specific exponent.
mathContext: Sanders' breakthrough came from bounding k-configurations — subsets where all pairwise sums remain in A. Fewer k-configurations force larger sum-avoiding subsets. Beker refined the k-configuration estimates to extract the specific exponent 1/68. The value 1/68 comes from optimizing multiple parameters in the combinatorial analysis.

title: k-Configurations
content: **IsKConfiguration A k B** requires B ⊆ A, |B| = k, and ∀ distinct b₁, b₂ ∈ B, b₁+b₂ ∈ A. This is the dual of sum-avoiding: all sums stay inside A rather than outside. If A has few k-configurations, then A must have large sum-avoiding subsets, connecting the two concepts via a counting duality.
mathContext: k-configurations are the key technical tool in Sanders' and Beker's work. The idea is that if a set A forces all large subsets to have many additive coincidences (i.e., many k-configurations), then A has special additive structure that can be exploited. Otherwise, random subsets are likely to be sum-avoiding.

title: Summary Theorem
content: **erdos_787_summary** packages three known results as a proved conjunction: (1) Sanders' lower bound (log n)^{1+c} ≪ g(n), (2) Ruzsa's upper bound g(n) ≪ exp(√(log n)), and (3) Beker's refined lower bound (log n)^{1+1/68-ε} ≪ g(n). The proof is ⟨sanders_2021_lower_bound, ruzsa_2005_upper_bound, beker_2025_lower_bound⟩.
mathContext: The three-part conjunction captures the complete state of knowledge: a qualitative lower bound (Sanders), the best upper bound (Ruzsa), and a quantitative lower bound with specific exponent (Beker). The enormous gap between parts (1)/(3) and part (2) is the main open challenge. This is one of the few problems where the lower and upper bounds differ by more than a polynomial factor.
